blocks.text: A portable filter strains out germs. It does **not** make every water safe. Read this first, then the section for your model.
What filters do and don't do

items: To remove **bacteria**, the filter's absolute pore size must be **0.3 micron or smaller**. For **parasites** (Giardia, Cryptosporidium), **1 micron or smaller**.
Most portable filters **do not remove viruses**. After filtering, add a disinfectant (chlorine, chlorine dioxide, or iodine), or boil.
Filters do **not** make water with fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive material safe.

blocks.text: Dissolved substances such as salt, fluoride and chlorine pass through Sawyer filters, and Katadyn says never to use the BeFree on seawater or brackish water.

**Freezing ruins hollow-fiber filters.** Ice inside the membrane can open cracks you can't see, and germs then pass through. Keep a wet filter above freezing (in a pocket or sleeping bag, close to your body). If it may have frozen, replace it.

blocks.alt: Squeeze filter, filter then backflush. 1, filter: dirty water goes through the filter into a clean container. Let dirty water settle or pour it through a cloth first, and do not attach the filter to a bucket that held chemicals. Most portable filters do not remove viruses, so after filtering boil the water or add chlorine, chlorine dioxide or iodine. 2, backflush: when flow slows, backflush straight into your bucket for about a minute, and the flow is restored. Backflush before first use, when flow starts to drop, before long storage, and when you take it out of storage, and after each bucket of water or at least once a day. Never backflush with dirty water. Freezing ruins the filter: keep a wet filter above freezing and replace it if it may have frozen. Safe range 32 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit.
blocks.caption: Using and backflushing a squeeze-style filter, as described below.

items: 0.1-micron filter. Sawyer says it removes bacteria, protozoa and cysts. It doesn't claim viruses.
**Backflush** (backwash) before first use, when flow starts to drop, before long storage, and when you take it out of storage. Do it straight into your bucket. It takes about a minute.
How often: after each bucket of water, or at least once a day. Clear water may only need it about every 1,000 gallons. Very muddy water: about every 10 gallons.
Don't backwash with dirty water. If you did, run at least 1 gallon through and throw it out before drinking from it.
Safe temperature range: 32°F to 140°F. Replace the filter if it may have frozen, been boiled, been dropped hard, or been overtightened.
How you know it's weak: flow slows, and a backwash restores it. Sawyer says there is no home integrity test. Replacing is cheaper than testing.
Don't attach it to a bucket that held chemicals. Pre-filter dirty water through a cloth or let it settle.
0.2-micron membrane **microfilter**. Rated for bacteria, parasites and microplastics. LifeStraw sells its virus-rated products as separate "ultrafilter" models, and this is not one of them.
Rated for up to 1,000 gallons (4,000 liters). It is a single-use unit with no replacement filter.
Water flow slows or stops when it reaches the end of its life.
LifeStraw says it is designed for germs, not chemicals or heavy metals.
Cleaning and storage: disinfect with a bleach solution, rinse, soak in salt water (saline), and store cool and dry. Follow the printed manual for the steps.
Freezing: ice in the membrane can expand the pores and ruin the filter. Replace it if it froze.
0.02-micron **ultrafilter**. LifeStraw lists 99.999% of viruses, 99.999999% of bacteria and 99.999% of parasites removed.
Rated for up to 4,755 gallons (18,000 liters). Maximum flow is 3.1 gallons (12 liters) per hour. The dirty-water tank holds 2 liters.
It does **not** remove chlorine or fluoride.
Before long storage, run about 2 liters of clean water with 2 teaspoons of household bleach through it, let it sit overnight, then rinse out all chlorine and dry the parts.
After long storage: fill the tank and open the red tap for 5 seconds to clear trapped air.
Check the manual for routine cleaning steps.
0.1-micron hollow-fiber membrane. Reduces bacteria and protozoan cysts. It **does not remove viruses**.

Use fresh, clear water. **Never** use it for seawater, brackish water or chemically contaminated water, such as water near large agricultural operations or mine ponds. It does not remove chemicals or radioactive material.
**Do not use in freezing conditions.** A frozen membrane can let germs through.
If viruses might be present, add Micropur tablets or boil the water for about 1 minute.
Cleaning: **shake or swish** the membrane in fresh water every 5 liters, or when flow is slow. Don't rinse it sideways under running water and don't touch the fibers.
Replace after **1,000 liters (264 gallons)**, or sooner if flow slows or stops and shake/swish doesn't fix it.
Integrity test: wet the membrane, then try to blow air through the drink nozzle. If you **can** blow air through, the fibers are broken. Stop using it and replace the membrane.
Before long storage, disinfect with 1 Micropur tablet (or 4 drops of household bleach) in filtered water, squeeze it through, and let it air-dry. After storage, flush with 2 liters.
Performance depends on the exact elements installed. Black Berkey elements are rated at roughly 3,000 gallons each (6,000 per pair). Phoenix elements, about 2,750 each.
**Prime** new elements and follow the flushing directions for your element **before drinking**. Poor priming is a common cause of slow flow.
Replace when the rated gallons are used, an element is damaged, performance is in doubt, or flow stays poor after cleaning and re-priming. Slow flow alone doesn't mean it's used up.
Cleaning: **no soap** on Black Berkey elements. Gently scrub the outside under cool running water with a new Scotch-Brite-type pad, then re-prime.
**Never let a wet element freeze.** Unused for 4 to 15 days: Phoenix instructions say to keep them damp in a sealed bag in the fridge.
Source water: Berkey's Phoenix guidance is for treated municipal water. Don't assume it disinfects untreated lake, stream or well water.
During a boil-water advisory, a filter does not replace boiling. Don't pour boiling water into the system.
Black Berkey replacements were out of normal U.S. supply when this was checked. Know how old your elements are.
Filter first. Cloudy water makes bleach and tablets work less well.
Then boil the filtered water, or treat it with bleach (see the bleach guide) or chlorine dioxide tablets.
Do this any time viruses might be present: sewage, floods, a boil advisory, or if your filter doesn't list viruses.
